title: His death, 1839
hookLine: when he died, several queens and servants burned on his pyre, against the Gurus' teaching

lines: THE LION OF THE PUNJAB DIES.
cards: The man who built the kingdom is old now. Strokes have taken much of his speech. In his last days, tradition says, he gave away gifts and treasure, and his court gathered around him in Lahore.
Then the Lion of the Punjab died, and the city mourned. What happened at his funeral is part of this story, and Sikh histories tell it honestly, because the Gurus had already spoken to it.

teach.h: QUEENS AND SERVANTS ON THE PYRE.
teach.b: At his cremation, several of his queens and some serving women burned with him on the pyre. This was sati, an old custom in parts of India, in which a widow died on her husband's funeral fire.
Histories record it, and Sikh tellings of it are full of sorrow.

teach.h: GURU AMAR DAS HAD SPOKEN AGAINST IT.
teach.b: Long before, Guru Amar Das had spoken plainly. In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, he says that women who burn themselves with their husbands' bodies are not truly called satis.

The true sati, he says, is one who lives on in goodness and contentment, and honors the Lord. The Gurus spoke against the custom, and Sikh tradition remembers Guru Amar Das working to end it among his followers.
So here is a hard thing. The kingdom ruled in the Khalsa's name, and yet at its founder's funeral, a practice the Gurus had rejected went ahead.

teach.h: THE COURT FELL SHORT OF THE GURU.
teach.b: An old custom was stronger, that day, than the Guru's word, and Sikh histories say plainly that the court fell short of the Gurus' teaching.
You don't have to make a hard truth smaller, or make it the whole story either.
The Maharaja who gave gold to the Harmandir and mercy to his enemies is the same man at whose funeral this happened. Both are true, and holding both is part of telling history with honesty.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's funeral honestly, and point to Guru Amar Das's hymn rejecting sati as the Gurus' teaching that the court failed to follow.

games.q: the founder of the Khalsa's kingdom has died. an old custom says his widows should die on his pyre. the Gurus taught against it. what happened?
o: the court followed the Gurus and stopped it.
the custom went ahead, against the Gurus' teaching.
games.why: several queens and serving women burned on the pyre. Sikhs say plainly that the court fell short of the Guru's word.

practice: Bring to mind the women who died that day, without names, just as people, and keep a moment of silence for them.
Then, if you like, let a hard truth in a story you love sit beside what's good in it, without arguing and without hurrying past. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: His death. The end of the Maharaja's life, and the funeral where queens and servants died on his pyre, against what Guru Amar Das had taught.

carryVoice: Your line: even kings fell short. The good stays true, and so does this. See you tomorrow.
